Rose___Healthy.description: The rose foliage appears vibrant, rich green, and robust with no detectable fungal lesions, pests, or physiological stress.
visual_symptoms: Lush, glossy deep-green leaves with crisp serrated edges.
Firm, sturdy stems without cankers or discoloration.
Uniform leaf pigmentation with no necrotic lesions or powdery residue.
Rose___Healthy.confidence_disclaimer: The plant is showing optimal health indicators. Routine seasonal monitoring is recommended to sustain vigorous blooming.
immediate_actions: Maintain consistent routine care.
Inspect underside of leaves weekly for early signs of aphids or spot spores.
Deadhead faded blooms above a 5-leaflet leaf to stimulate repeat blooming.

watering.frequency: 1-2 times per week (adjust for summer heat)
watering.method: Deep watering directly at the base or through drip irrigation. Avoid wetting leaves.
watering.schedule_tips: Water in the early morning to allow any accidental moisture on leaves to evaporate quickly.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: 6 to 8 hours of direct, unfiltered sunlight daily.
sunlight_environment.airflow: Ensure good open spacing (2-3 feet) between plants for natural cross-ventilation.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Thrives in temperatures between 18°C–28°C (65°F–82°F) with moderate humidity.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Rich, well-draining loamy soil enriched with well-rotted organic compost.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Apply balanced slow-release rose fertilizer (NPK 10-10-10 or 12-15-10) every 4-6 weeks during blooming season.

organic: Apply preventative neem oil spray (0.5% concentration) once a month during spring.
Top-dress soil with organic compost tea to bolster natural root microbiome.
chemical: No chemical interventions necessary for healthy plants.

prevention: Prune crossing internal branches in early spring to encourage open vase structure.
Mulch 2-3 inches around the base (keeping 2 inches away from main stem) to retain moisture and suppress weeds.
Clean and sanitize pruning shears with 70% isopropyl alcohol.
checklist_tasks: Check soil moisture 2 inches deep before watering
Deadhead spent blooms to encourage new buds
Perform weekly underside leaf inspection
Apply slow-release rose fertilizer once a month

Rose___Black_Spot.description: A destructive fungal disease that manifests as circular black spots with feathery, fringed margins on the upper leaf surface, eventually causing rapid yellowing and premature defoliation.
visual_symptoms: Circular black spots (up to 1/2 inch across) with fringed, feathery margins.
Bright yellow halos forming around the dark spots as infected tissue deteriorates.
Premature leaf drop starting from lower branches and working upwards.
Rose___Black_Spot.confidence_disclaimer: Symptoms can mimic Cercospora leaf spot or physiological yellowing. High humidity and prolonged leaf wetness strongly favor Diplocarpon rosae development.
immediate_actions: Prune off all visibly infected leaves immediately using sanitized shears.
Rake up and safely discard all fallen leaves from the soil surface (do NOT compost diseased leaves).
Isolate overhead sprinkler watering immediately.

watering.frequency: Water only when top 2 inches of soil are dry.
watering.method: Water strictly at soil level using a soaker hose or watering wand. Keep foliage completely dry.
watering.schedule_tips: Always water early in the morning so accidental splashes dry before midday.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Full sun (minimum 6+ hours). Direct sunlight accelerates leaf drying and inhibits fungal spore germination.
sunlight_environment.airflow: Prune center canes to open the plant canopy and improve airflow.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Fungus thrives between 20°C–27°C with >80% relative humidity. Maximum ventilation is critical.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Loamy, well-draining soil with organic matter.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers during active infection (excess soft growth is vulnerable). Use potassium-rich fertilizers to strengthen cell walls.

organic: Spray with cold-pressed Neem Oil (1 oz per gallon of water) every 7-10 days in the evening.
Apply Potassium Bicarbonate spray (1 tbsp potassium bicarbonate + 1 tsp liquid castile soap per gallon water).
Apply Bio-fungicide containing Bacillus amyloliquefaciens or Bacillus subtilis.
chemical: Apply broad-spectrum systemic fungicide containing Myclobutanil, Tebuconazole, or Chlorothalonil.
Spray every 10-14 days during wet/humid weather, alternating active ingredients to prevent resistance.

prevention: Apply a 2-3 inch fresh layer of cedar or pine bark mulch over soil to trap remaining soil fungal spores.
Sterilize pruning tools with rubbing alcohol or 10% bleach solution between every plant cut.
Choose disease-resistant rose cultivars for future plantings (e.g. Knock Out, Rugosa hybrids).
checklist_tasks: Prune and dispose of all spotted leaves (in trash, not compost)
Sanitize pruning shears with 70% alcohol
Switch strictly to base watering (never wet leaves)
Apply organic neem oil or potassium bicarbonate spray
Add fresh 2-inch mulch layer to prevent soil spore splash

Rose___Powdery_Mildew.description: A prevalent fungal condition causing a distinctive talcum-like white or grayish powdery coating across tender young leaves, shoots, and flower buds.
visual_symptoms: White to grayish powdery coating on upper leaf surface, young shoots, and sepals.
Curling, blistering, or distortion of young leaves.
Unopened flower buds failing to open or blooming with deformed petals.
Rose___Powdery_Mildew.confidence_disclaimer: Powdery mildew thrives in warm, dry daytime weather paired with cool, humid nights. Often confused with residue from hard water spray.
immediate_actions: Gently prune severely coated shoots and buds to lower spore concentration.
Relocate potted roses to high-sunlight, high-airflow locations.
Apply therapeutic spray before spores spread to new growth.

watering.frequency: Water thoroughly once or twice weekly.
watering.method: Water at root level. Keep foliage dry during humid periods.
watering.schedule_tips: Morning hydration ensures turgid, stress-resilient foliage.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Full direct sunlight (at least 6-8 hours daily). Shade significantly encourages mildew.
sunlight_environment.airflow: Maximize space around rose bushes. Thin out congested canes.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Warm days (22°C–30°C) with humid nights facilitate spore production.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Rich, well-aerated soil with adequate organic amendments.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Reduce high-nitrogen feeds which spur excessively tender succulent growth.

organic: Milk spray: Mix 1 part milk (dairy or whey) with 9 parts water and spray in full sunlight every 5-7 days.
Horticultural oil or Neem oil spray applied thoroughly over both sides of foliage.
Baking soda solution: 1 tbsp baking soda + 1/2 tsp dish soap in 1 gallon warm water.
chemical: Apply sulfur-based fungicide or Triforine / Myclobutanil.
CAUTION: Do not apply sulfur sprays within 30 days of oil sprays to prevent leaf scorch.

prevention: Maintain spacious planting distance for optimal air circulation.
Plant resistant varieties in locations with morning sun to dry overnight dew.
Avoid over-fertilizing with quick-release nitrogen in spring.
checklist_tasks: Prune distorted or heavily coated leaves
Move plant to full sun location with good air circulation
Spray diluted milk solution or neem oil in morning
Hold off on high-nitrogen fertilizer

Rose___Aphid_Infestation.description: Small, soft-bodied sap-sucking insects (green, pink, or black) clustered heavily on tender young shoots, unopened flower buds, and undersides of new leaves.
visual_symptoms: Clusters of tiny green/pink pear-shaped insects on flower buds and stem tips.
Curled, puckered, or stunted new growth.
Sticky clear residue ('honeydew') on leaves, accompanied by black sooty mold.
Ant activity crawling up stems to farm honeydew.
Rose___Aphid_Infestation.confidence_disclaimer: Aphids reproduce rapidly in temperate spring conditions. Early detection makes non-chemical eradication straightforward.
immediate_actions: Blast clusters with a strong, direct jet of water from a garden hose nozzle.
Squish small localized colonies with gloved fingers.
Check underside of leaves and terminal buds.

watering.frequency: Normal watering schedule.
watering.method: Direct base watering.
watering.schedule_tips: Hydrate stressed plants so they recover sap loss faster.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Full sun (6+ hours). Healthy sun exposure builds tougher, insect-resistant leaf cuticle.
sunlight_environment.airflow: Normal open airflow.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Aphid population peaks in mild spring temps (18°C–24°C).

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Standard well-drained rose soil.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Pause heavy nitrogen fertilizer; excess nitrogen creates lush, soft succulent shoots that attract aphids.

organic: Insecticidal soap spray: Dilute 2 tbsp pure castile soap per quart of water, spray directly onto pests.
Neem oil spray (1-2% solution): Disrupts insect feeding and growth cycles.
Introduce or encourage beneficial predators (ladybugs, lacewings, hoverfly larvae).
chemical: Apply Pyrethrin-based spray or Acetamiprid if infestation is out of control.
Avoid spraying blooming flowers to protect pollinating bees.

prevention: Plant companion plants like Marigolds, Alliums (garlic/chives), and Sweet Alyssum to repel aphids and attract predators.
Regularly inspect new spring shoots twice a week.
Control ant populations with sticky barriers around main stem base.
checklist_tasks: Hose down flower buds with strong water spray
Apply organic insecticidal soap or neem oil spray
Wipe away sticky honeydew to prevent black sooty mold
Pause high-nitrogen fertilization

Rose___Rust.description: A distinct fungal infection characterized by bright orange, powdery pustules on the lower leaf surface, paired with yellow flecks on the upper leaf surface.
visual_symptoms: Small, raised, powdery bright-orange or rusty-brown pustules on undersides of leaves.
Corresponding yellow-orange chlorotic spots on upper leaf surfaces.
Severe infections cause leaves to curl, dry up, and fall off prematurely.
Rose___Rust.confidence_disclaimer: Pustules become darker brown or black in late autumn as overwintering teliospores form.
immediate_actions: Remove and incinerate/bag all affected leaves immediately.
Avoid touching healthy leaves after handling rusted foliage.
Rake ground clean beneath rose shrubs.

watering.frequency: Regular watering at base.
watering.method: Strictly root zone watering with soaker hose. Zero overhead sprinkler use.
watering.schedule_tips: Water early in the morning.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Full sun (6-8 hours daily).
sunlight_environment.airflow: Prune interior branches to optimize air flow and decrease humidity around foliage.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Rust spores require free moisture for 2-4 hours to germinate at 18°C–21°C.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Rich loamy soil with high drainage.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Maintain balanced potassium and phosphorus; avoid excess nitrogen.

organic: Spray sulfur or copper soap fungicide at first sign of orange pustules.
Apply Bacillus subtilis biofungicide weekly.
chemical: Apply systemic fungicides containing Tebuconazole, Mancozeb, or Myclobutanil.
Repeat applications every 10-14 days during wet spells.

prevention: Maintain clean bed beneath roses with fresh mulch every spring.
Disinfect pruning tools with 70% alcohol.
Prune deadwood and thin canopy during winter dormancy.
checklist_tasks: Pick off and dispose of all orange-pustuled leaves
Sanitize hands and shears with disinfectant
Apply copper-based fungicide or sulfur spray
Ensure leaves remain dry during watering

Hibiscus___Healthy.description: Vibrant, glossy emerald green foliage with sturdy branching and vigorous flower bud formation.
visual_symptoms: Broad, dark green glossy leaves with even coloration.
Plump flower buds ready to bloom.
Active new shoot growth without leaf curling or yellowing.
Hibiscus___Healthy.confidence_disclaimer: Plant shows excellent health metrics. Regular tropical feeding and warmth maintain continuous flowering.
immediate_actions: Maintain consistent tropical care routine.
Provide ample warm sunshine and regular deep hydration.
Deadhead spent single-day flowers to keep plant clean.

watering.frequency: Daily during hot summer months; 2-3 times weekly in moderate weather.
watering.method: Deep, thorough soaking until water drains freely from pot or permeates root zone.
watering.schedule_tips: Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: 6+ hours of bright direct to slightly dappled afternoon sun.
sunlight_environment.airflow: Warm, gentle air movement. Protect from freezing winds or cold drafts (<10°C).
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Prefers 20°C–32°C (68°F–90°F) and 50%+ relative humidity.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Light, fluffy, highly porous potting mix with perlite, peat, and organic compost.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Hibiscus are potassium lovers! Use high-potassium fertilizer (e.g. NPK 17-5-24 or 9-3-13) with trace iron and magnesium.

organic: Routine monthly preventative neem oil application.
Foliar seaweed / kelp meal spray to boost flowering vigor.
chemical: No treatments required for healthy specimens.

prevention: Protect from temperatures below 10°C (50°F) by bringing indoors during winter.
Ensure container has multiple drainage holes to prevent root rot.
checklist_tasks: Water thoroughly when top 1 inch of soil dries
Feed with high-potassium hibiscus fertilizer
Ensure minimum 6 hours of bright sunlight
Remove spent blossoms

Hibiscus___Leaf_Blight.condition_name: Hibiscus Leaf Blight / Fungal Spot (Alternaria / Cercospora)
Hibiscus___Leaf_Blight.description: Fungal leaf blight causing water-soaked, irregular brown or necrotic tan spots with dark margins across hibiscus leaves, leading to widespread leaf yellowing and dropping.
visual_symptoms: Irregular brown or grayish lesions with dark purple-brown margins.
Concentric rings or 'target' patterns inside larger necrotic spots.
Yellowing around diseased areas and sudden lower leaf shedding.
Hibiscus___Leaf_Blight.confidence_disclaimer: Often triggered by overhead watering, warm humid nights, and crowded foliage.
immediate_actions: Clip off all blighted leaves and collect fallen debris immediately.
Cease any overhead misting or spraying of leaves.
Move pot to a breezier, sunnier spot to accelerate surface drying.

watering.frequency: Water when top 1-2 inches feel dry.
watering.method: Water base directly. Ensure drainage saucers are emptied after watering.
watering.schedule_tips: Early morning watering only.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Full sun to bright indirect light (6+ hours).
sunlight_environment.airflow: Position plant where air circulates freely around all sides.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Ensure good ventilation during humid summer spells.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Well-aerated potting mix with excellent drainage.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Temporarily suspend heavy fertilization until new healthy growth emerges.

organic: Apply liquid Copper Octanoate fungicide spray thoroughly.
Neem oil spray (1%) every 7 days in late afternoon.
chemical: Broad-spectrum fungicide containing Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb.
Repeat application every 7-10 days until leaf spotting subsides.

prevention: Never splash soil or water onto foliage.
Prune dense inner branches to let sunlight penetrate the interior.
Sanitize pruning blades with isopropyl alcohol.
checklist_tasks: Prune affected spotted leaves and discard
Disinfect pruning tools
Spray with copper fungicide or neem oil
Ensure bottom drainage is clear and unblocked

Hibiscus___Aphid_Infestation.description: Sap-feeding insects attacking the soft growing tips and buds of tropical hibiscus, causing bud drop, twisted foliage, and sticky honeydew excretion.
visual_symptoms: Dense clusters of small green, black, or cottony white insects on bud stems.
Flower buds turning yellow and dropping off before opening.
Distorted, stunted new leaves.
Sticky honeydew with sooty mold growth on upper leaf surfaces.
Hibiscus___Aphid_Infestation.confidence_disclaimer: Mealybugs appear as white cottony masses in leaf axils; aphids appear as tiny shiny pear-shaped bugs on stems.
immediate_actions: Wash affected tips with a targeted strong stream of water.
Dab individual mealybugs with a cotton swab dipped in 70% rubbing alcohol.
Isolate the plant from other indoor/outdoor plants.

watering.frequency: Maintain steady soil moisture.
watering.method: Water thoroughly at root level.
watering.schedule_tips: Avoid water stress which weakens plant defenses.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Full sun (6+ hours).
sunlight_environment.airflow: Good air movement.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Pests flourish in sheltered, warm, dry indoor or patio environments.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Porous, rich soil mix.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Stop high nitrogen feeding which fuels rapid pest population surges.

organic: Insecticidal soap spray (covering undersides of leaves and flower buds).
Pure cold-pressed neem oil (applied every 5-7 days for 3 cycles).
Horticultural mineral oil spray.
chemical: Systemic insecticide granules (Imidacloprid/Dinotefuran) for severe container infestations.
Pyrethrin spray for fast knockdown.

prevention: Inspect leaf axils and bud stems weekly.
Wipe down stems regularly with diluted castile soap solution.
Introduce beneficial green lacewings.
checklist_tasks: Dab cottony pests with alcohol swab
Spray entire plant with insecticidal soap or neem oil
Rinse sticky honeydew from lower leaves
Check underside of flower buds

Hibiscus___Iron_Chlorosis.description: A physiological nutrient deficiency where leaves turn pale yellow or ivory while the leaf veins remain distinctly dark green, caused by lack of available iron or alkaline soil pH.
visual_symptoms: Interveinal chlorosis: leaf tissue turns yellow, lime-green, or whitish while veins stay sharply dark green.
Youngest leaves at shoot tips are affected first.
In severe cases, leaf margins may brown, curl, and die back.
Hibiscus___Iron_Chlorosis.confidence_disclaimer: Can be caused by true soil iron deficiency OR soil pH above 7.0 which locks up iron availability. Overwatering can also mimic iron chlorosis by rotting feeder roots.
immediate_actions: Check soil pH with a test kit (if pH > 7.0, acidify with sulfur or peat).
Apply foliar spray of chelated iron (Fe-EDTA or Fe-EDDHA) for rapid green-up.
Verify that roots are not sitting in waterlogged, suffocated soil.

watering.frequency: Allow top 1-2 inches of soil to dry slightly before watering.
watering.method: Ensure complete water drainage to promote healthy oxygen exchange in the root zone.
watering.schedule_tips: Overly wet soil prevents roots from absorbing iron ions.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Full sun (6+ hours).
sunlight_environment.airflow: Normal airflow.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Cold soil temperatures (<15°C) can temporarily restrict iron uptake.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Acidic to neutral, rich potting mix.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Apply high-potassium hibiscus fertilizer with chelated micronutrients (Iron, Magnesium, Zinc, Manganese).

organic: Top-dress with organic compost, peat moss, or worm castings to gently lower pH.
Apply liquid kelp meal and chelated iron foliar drench.
chemical: Drench soil with Chelated Iron (Fe-EDDHA for alkaline soil, Fe-EDTA for acidic soil).
Apply Epsom salts (Magnesium Sulfate: 1 tbsp/gallon water) if magnesium deficiency is also suspected.

prevention: Maintain soil pH strictly between 6.0 and 6.5.
Avoid using hard, alkaline tap water (collect rainwater if tap water is heavily mineralized).
Use fertilizers formulated specifically with chelated trace minerals for tropical hibiscus.
checklist_tasks: Test soil pH and adjust toward 6.0-6.5
Apply chelated iron foliar spray or root drench
Ensure pot is draining properly and not waterlogged
Feed with balanced hibiscus micronutrient fertilizer

Marigold___Healthy.description: Bushy, aromatic deep green feathery foliage with bright, showy golden-orange flower heads.
visual_symptoms: Deep green, finely divided pinnate foliage.
Sturdy erect stems with abundant flower buds.
No webbing, spotting, or leaf browning.
Marigold___Healthy.confidence_disclaimer: Marigolds are naturally hardy, pest-repellent garden flowers. Keep in full sun for nonstop blossoms.
immediate_actions: Deadhead spent flowers regularly to stimulate continuous bud production.
Maintain consistent sunlight exposure.

watering.frequency: 1-2 times a week when soil is dry to the touch.
watering.method: Water at the base. Marigolds prefer soaking then drying out slightly.
watering.schedule_tips: Avoid keeping soil constantly soggy.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Full direct sunlight (at least 6-8 hours daily for maximum blooms).
sunlight_environment.airflow: Excellent open air circulation.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Thrives in warm temperatures (20°C–32°C / 68°F–90°F).

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Moderately fertile, well-draining garden soil.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Low to moderate fertilization. Avoid excessive fertilizer, which promotes lush leaves at the expense of flowers.

organic: Marigolds naturally produce alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes.
chemical: No chemical treatment required.

prevention: Space plants 8-12 inches apart to prevent humidity buildup.
Pinch back young seedlings to encourage bushier growth.
checklist_tasks: Deadhead spent flower heads to stimulate new blooms
Water at the base when topsoil feels dry
Keep in full sun position

Marigold___Alternaria_Blight.description: A prevalent fungal blight in marigolds causing dark brown, water-soaked target spots on leaves and petal blight on blossoms.
visual_symptoms: Small circular reddish-brown to dark brown spots on lower leaves.
Spots enlarge with concentric zonate rings ('target-board' appearance).
Blossoms turn brown, rot, and wither before fully opening.
Marigold___Alternaria_Blight.confidence_disclaimer: Common during prolonged rainfall or overhead irrigation in summer.
immediate_actions: Snip and discard blighted leaves and rotting flower heads.
Discontinue all sprinkler or overhead hose watering.
Thin congested plants to promote rapid drying.

watering.frequency: Allow surface soil to dry out between waterings.
watering.method: Apply water directly to the soil bed around the roots.
watering.schedule_tips: Morning irrigation only.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Full sun (6+ hours daily).
sunlight_environment.airflow: Ensure wide spacing between plants.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Warm, humid conditions (24°C–30°C) accelerate spore germination.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Fast-draining sandy loam or garden soil.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Maintain balanced nutrition; avoid excessive nitrogen.

organic: Spray with organic liquid Copper fungicide.
Apply biological fungicide containing Trichoderma harzianum or Bacillus subtilis.
chemical: Spray with Mancozeb, Chlorothalonil, or Azoxystrobin at 7-10 day intervals.

prevention: Space seedlings 10-12 inches apart to avoid crowded canopies.
Use drip irrigation or soaker hoses.
Practice crop rotation; do not plant marigolds in the exact same spot consecutively.
checklist_tasks: Remove all infected foliage and flowers
Spray with copper fungicide or Mancozeb
Switch strictly to ground watering
Sterilize shears after pruning

Marigold___Powdery_Mildew.description: White powdery fungal mycelium covering the finely divided leaves and stems of marigolds, causing foliage to turn brittle and dry.
visual_symptoms: White dusty patches expanding over leaves, stems, and flower bracts.
Foliage turning grayish-yellow, curling upward, and drying out.
Reduced flowering and overall plant stunting.
Marigold___Powdery_Mildew.confidence_disclaimer: Common in late summer and autumn as nights turn cooler and days remain warm.
immediate_actions: Trim off heavily infected lower foliage.
Ensure plants receive full morning sun.
Apply an organic anti-fungal spray.

watering.frequency: Water when top 1 inch of soil is dry.
watering.method: Water at base level.
watering.schedule_tips: Water in early morning.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Full direct sun (6-8 hours daily).
sunlight_environment.airflow: Provide high-airflow spacing.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Avoid shaded, humid corners.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Well-drained soil.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Avoid high nitrogen feeds.

organic: Spray with potassium bicarbonate or baking soda (1 tsp per quart water + drop of soap).
Neem oil spray (0.5-1%) applied in evening.
chemical: Apply sulfur dust or Myclobutanil fungicide.

prevention: Plant marigolds in unshaded areas with maximum sunlight.
Thin foliage to ensure sunlight reaches the lower canopy.
checklist_tasks: Prune dusty coated leaves
Spray baking soda or neem solution
Relocate to full sun position

Marigold___Spider_Mites.description: Microscopic arachnid pests that pierce plant cells and suck out chlorophyll, causing fine yellow stippling and delicate silky webbing across leaves and buds.
visual_symptoms: Fine yellow/bronze stippling (tiny dots) across upper leaf surfaces.
Delicate, silky webbing spun between leaf axils and flower heads.
Leaves turning bronze, brittle, paper-dry, and dropping.
Tiny moving specks visible on the underside of leaves when tapped over white paper.
Marigold___Spider_Mites.confidence_disclaimer: Spider mites proliferate explosively in hot, dry, dusty conditions.
immediate_actions: Spray plant thoroughly with a forceful cold water spray to dislodge mites and destroy webbing.
Isolate heavily infested plants.
Mist surroundings to elevate ambient humidity.

watering.frequency: Keep soil evenly hydrated; drought stress makes marigolds hyper-susceptible.
watering.method: Base watering + occasional cold foliar wash to deter mites.
watering.schedule_tips: Do not let soil become bone-dry in summer.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Full sun, but provide light afternoon shade during extreme 38°C+ heat waves.
sunlight_environment.airflow: Ensure good ventilation without hot dry winds.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Mites thrive at temperatures above 30°C and <30% humidity.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Moisture-retentive yet well-draining soil.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Balanced feeding; excess nitrogen encourages mite reproduction.

organic: Insecticidal soap spray (ensure complete coverage of leaf undersides).
Neem oil or Rosemary-oil based miticide.
Release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis).
chemical: Apply specific miticide/acaricide (Abamectin, Bifenazate).

prevention: Keep plants well-watered and avoid dusty garden conditions.
Regularly wash undersides of leaves during dry spells.
Mulch around base to conserve soil moisture.
checklist_tasks: Hose down plant and wipe away webbing
Spray insecticidal soap on undersides of leaves
Water deeply to eliminate drought stress
Repeat treatment in 4-5 days to target newly hatched eggs

Jasmine___Healthy.description: Lush, glossy deep green leaves climbing vigorously with clusters of intensely fragrant star-shaped white flowers.
visual_symptoms: Rich dark green glossy foliage with vibrant twining stems.
Prolific fragrant white flower clusters.
No pest webbing, rust spots, or chlorosis.
Jasmine___Healthy.confidence_disclaimer: Jasmine thrives in warm sunlight and well-aerated soil. Regular pruning after flowering maintains thick bushy growth.
immediate_actions: Maintain trellis support for climbing varieties.
Deadhead spent flower clusters to stimulate lateral branching.

watering.frequency: Water when top 1 inch of soil feels dry.
watering.method: Deep, thorough soaking at root base.
watering.schedule_tips: Reduce watering slightly in winter dormancy.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Full sun to partial shade (at least 6 hours of bright light).
sunlight_environment.airflow: Good open ventilation.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Warm climate (18°C–30°C). Protect from frost.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Rich, loamy, fast-draining soil with compost.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Apply balanced organic fertilizer (NPK 10-10-10) or phosphorus-rich bloom booster twice a month during spring and summer.

organic: Routine seaweed extract foliar spray.
chemical: No chemical treatments needed.

prevention: Prune back after main blooming cycle to prevent tangling.
Mulch root zone to keep roots cool in summer.
checklist_tasks: Inspect climbing canes and tie to trellis
Water when topsoil feels dry
Apply balanced fertilizer during blooming season

Jasmine___Leaf_Rust.description: Fungal rust causing yellow-orange blisters and hypertrophied (swollen/distorted) orange spore pustules on leaves, petioles, and tender green stems.
visual_symptoms: Bright yellow-orange or reddish pustules on leaves and green stems.
Swelling, twisting, and abnormal distortion of young shoots.
Premature leaf drop and drying of flower buds.
Jasmine___Leaf_Rust.confidence_disclaimer: Rust spores spread rapidly during humid rainy periods.
immediate_actions: Prune away all distorted twigs and rusted leaves.
Bag and dispose of clipped infected material safely.
Disinfect shears after every cut.

watering.frequency: Water at base when top 2 inches dry.
watering.method: Root zone irrigation only.
watering.schedule_tips: Keep vine foliage dry.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Full sunlight (6+ hours).
sunlight_environment.airflow: Thin dense vine tangles to allow air and light through the canopy.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Ensure rapid leaf drying after rain.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Well-aerated soil.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer.

organic: Apply Copper Oxychloride or wettable sulfur spray.
Neem oil spray (1%) every 10 days.
chemical: Spray with systemic fungicides like Hexaconazole, Propiconazole, or Mancozeb.

prevention: Regular seasonal pruning of interior old wood.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
Clean ground beneath vines of fallen leaves.
checklist_tasks: Prune and dispose of swollen, rusted stems
Sanitize pruning tools
Apply copper-based or Hexaconazole spray
Ensure foliage stays dry during watering

Jasmine___Bud_Borer_Damage.description: Small caterpillars that bore into unopened flower buds, feeding internally, causing buds to turn pale, dry up, fail to open, and show tiny entry holes with frass.
visual_symptoms: Flower buds showing tiny circular entry bore-holes with dark frass (droppings).
Buds turning brownish-pink or translucent and dropping before opening.
Silken webbing binding several flower buds together.
Jasmine___Bud_Borer_Damage.confidence_disclaimer: Significant cause of flower loss in garden jasmine during budding seasons.
immediate_actions: Hand-pick and destroy all webbed, bored, or discolored flower buds.
Examine buds closely in early morning or dusk for caterpillar presence.

watering.frequency: Normal watering schedule.
watering.method: Direct base watering.
watering.schedule_tips: Maintain standard hydration.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Full sun (6+ hours).
sunlight_environment.airflow: Open airflow.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Pest activity peaks in warm, humid flowering months.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Rich loamy soil.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Maintain balanced feeding.

organic: Spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt - Kurstaki) spray; highly effective against caterpillars without harming pollinators.
Apply Spinosad spray in late evening when bees are not foraging.
Neem seed kernel extract (NSKE 5%) spray.
chemical: Apply Chlorantraniliprole or Emamectin benzoate for heavy commercial infestations.

prevention: Rake soil around base of plants to expose pupae to birds and sunlight.
Spray Bt preventatively when flower bud clusters begin to form.
Install yellow sticky traps to detect adult moth presence.
checklist_tasks: Pick and discard all bored flower buds
Apply biological Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray in evening
Rake and cultivate soil around base to disturb pupae

Jasmine___Nutrient_Deficiency.description: Generalized yellowing of older or younger foliage accompanied by slow growth, weak stems, and sparse flower bud production.
visual_symptoms: Uniform pale yellowing of older lower leaves (Nitrogen deficiency).
Yellowing between veins on newer leaves (Iron / Magnesium deficiency).
Stunted vine elongation and reduced floral fragrance.
Jasmine___Nutrient_Deficiency.confidence_disclaimer: Deficiency can result from depleted potting soil, improper pH locking nutrients, or root binding in containers.
immediate_actions: Check if plant is root-bound in container; repot if necessary.
Apply balanced liquid foliar feed with micronutrients.
Test and adjust soil pH.

watering.frequency: Water when top 1 inch feels dry.
watering.method: Water thoroughly until runoff occurs.
watering.schedule_tips: Ensure pot drains freely.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Bright sun (6 hours daily).
sunlight_environment.airflow: Normal airflow.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Optimal growing temp: 20°C–28°C.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Nutrient-rich, well-aerated potting mix with compost and vermicompost.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Apply balanced water-soluble fertilizer (NPK 19-19-19) plus chelated trace elements (Fe, Mg, Zn).

organic: Top-dress with well-rotted cow manure, vermicompost, or blood meal.
Foliar spray with liquid seaweed / fish emulsion.
chemical: Apply Epsom salts (Magnesium Sulfate: 1 tbsp/gallon) + Chelated Iron drench.

prevention: Top-dress containers with fresh compost every spring.
Maintain regular bi-weekly feeding during active growing seasons.
checklist_tasks: Apply balanced NPK fertilizer with micronutrients
Drench with Epsom salt solution for magnesium boost
Check root system if potted and upsize if root-bound

General_Flower___Healthy.description: The flowering plant displays robust green leaves, intact stems, and active bud or blossom development with no signs of pathological infection.
visual_symptoms: Vibrant green, firm foliage with natural luster.
No necrotic lesions, fungal mildew, pest clusters, or severe wilting.
Sturdy stems supporting healthy flower buds.
General_Flower___Healthy.confidence_disclaimer: Plant shows healthy physiological characteristics. Follow species-specific maintenance.
immediate_actions: Continue standard watering and lighting routine.
Deadhead spent flowers to prolong blooming duration.

watering.frequency: When top 1-2 inches of soil feel dry to the touch.
watering.method: Water deeply at base level, avoiding excessive leaf wetness.
watering.schedule_tips: Morning watering is best.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Adequate sunlight (4-8 hours depending on plant variety).
sunlight_environment.airflow: Ensure good space around the pot or garden bed.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Maintain comfortable room/garden temperatures (18°C–28°C).

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Well-draining, organically enriched soil.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Apply balanced all-purpose flowering plant fertilizer once every 3-4 weeks.

organic: Preventative neem oil or compost tea monthly.
chemical: None needed.

prevention: Sanitize pruning tools before making cuts.
Ensure containers have functional drainage holes.
checklist_tasks: Check soil moisture before watering
Deadhead faded blooms
Apply all-purpose flower fertilizer monthly

General_Flower___Fungal_Leaf_Spot.description: Fungal pathogen infection causing discrete brown, black, or tan spots with yellow halos across the foliage, often accelerating leaf drop.
visual_symptoms: Circular or angular brown/black necrotic spots on leaves.
Yellow halo or ring encircling each spot.
Spots may coalesce into large dead patches causing leaf drop.
General_Flower___Fungal_Leaf_Spot.confidence_disclaimer: Fungal leaf spots are predominantly triggered by overhead water splashing and stagnant humidity.
immediate_actions: Remove and safely discard all spotted leaves.
Stop wetting the foliage when watering.
Increase distance between neighboring plants.

watering.frequency: Water only when topsoil is dry.
watering.method: Water directly at soil level using a narrow-spout watering can.
watering.schedule_tips: Always water in early morning.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Bright sunlight to facilitate foliage drying.
sunlight_environment.airflow: Provide high-ventilation placement.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Lower ambient humidity around foliage.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Free-draining potting medium.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Avoid high nitrogen feeds during active flare-up.

organic: Spray organic Copper fungicide or Neem oil (1%) every 7-10 days.
Apply potassium bicarbonate spray solution.
chemical: Broad-spectrum fungicide containing Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb.

prevention: Never water plants from above.
Disinfect scissors/pruners with alcohol.
Apply clean mulch over soil surface to prevent spore splash.
checklist_tasks: Prune off spotted leaves and discard
Sanitize scissors with alcohol
Spray with copper fungicide or neem oil
Water only at root base

General_Flower___Overwatering_Stress.description: Physiological stress caused by persistently waterlogged soil, depriving roots of oxygen and causing root rot, edema, and yellowing limp leaves.
visual_symptoms: Lower leaves turning pale yellow, soft, and limp despite wet soil.
Soil surface remaining soggy, mossy, or emitting a stale sour odor.
Stems feeling soft or blackened near the soil line (early stem rot).
Blister-like bumps (edema) on the undersides of leaves.
General_Flower___Overwatering_Stress.confidence_disclaimer: Yellow leaves from overwatering are often mistaken for underwatering or nutrient deficiency. Always feel soil depth before adding water!
immediate_actions: Stop watering immediately and allow the soil to dry out thoroughly.
Empty any standing water sitting in the pot saucer or drip tray.
If severe, unpot the plant, inspect roots, snip off black mushy roots, and repot in fresh dry soil.

watering.frequency: Strictly withhold water until the top 2-3 inches of soil feel completely dry.
watering.method: When watering resumes, water deeply until slight drainage occurs, then do not water again until dry.
watering.schedule_tips: Never water on a rigid calendar schedule; always check soil moisture first.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Move to a brighter location with warm indirect sun to help the plant transpire excess water.
sunlight_environment.airflow: Increase air movement around pot base.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Ensure good drainage and air flow.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Porous, aerated mix with perlite, coarse sand, or pumice for drainage.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Do NOT fertilize a water-stressed plant; damaged root tips will burn easily.

organic: Drench soil with diluted 3% Hydrogen Peroxide (1 part 3% H2O2 to 4 parts water) to oxygenate root zone and kill anaerobic bacteria/fungi.
Dust trimmed root ends with cinnamon powder or sulfur before repotting.
chemical: Apply systemic anti-root rot fungicide (e.g. Mefenoxam or Fosetyl-Al) for high-value specimens.

prevention: Always ensure pots have open drainage holes.
Use well-draining potting soil with 25-30% perlite.
Use the 'finger test' or a moisture meter before watering.
checklist_tasks: Empty standing water from pot saucer immediately
Withhold watering until top 2-3 inches are dry
Ensure pot drainage holes are unobstructed
Pause all fertilizer until new growth appears

General_Flower___Dehydration_Stress.description: Acute water shortage causing loss of cell turgidity, wilting, crispy brown leaf margins, and premature flower bud shedding.
visual_symptoms: Drooping, limp stems and wilting leaves that feel paper-thin or dry.
Crispy, brown, curled leaf tips and edges.
Soil pulling away from the inside edges of the pot; bone-dry root ball.
Flower buds and open blossoms drying up and dropping off.
General_Flower___Dehydration_Stress.confidence_disclaimer: Distinguished from overwatering by dry, crumbly soil and crispy leaf texture rather than soft, soggy yellow leaves.
immediate_actions: Give the plant an immediate bottom-watering soak (place pot in a basin of water for 20-30 minutes until soil rehydrates).
Move out of scorching midday direct sun until leaves regain turgidity.
Do NOT apply heavy fertilizer while plant is dehydrated.

watering.frequency: Water consistently as soon as the top 1 inch of soil is dry.
watering.method: Thorough deep watering until water runs out the drainage holes, ensuring hydrophobic dry pockets are saturated.
watering.schedule_tips: Water in the morning or early evening.

sunlight_environment.sunlight: Temporary filtered light until recovered, then return to normal sunlight.
sunlight_environment.airflow: Moderate airflow; avoid placing directly in the path of hot air blowers or air conditioning.
sunlight_environment.temperature_humidity: Increase humidity around the plant if indoor air is dry.

soil_nutrition.soil_type: Moisture-retentive yet well-drained soil rich in organic matter / coco coir.
soil_nutrition.fertilizer: Resume gentle feeding only after plant is fully rehydrated and producing new growth.

organic: Add a 1-inch top dressing of organic compost or mulch to retain soil moisture.
Foliar mist with pure water during recovery.
chemical: None required; hydration resolves dehydration stress.

prevention: Establish a regular soil check routine (e.g. check every 2 days in summer).
Add mulch to reduce soil moisture evaporation.
Use self-watering pots or olla pots for moisture-sensitive flowering plants.
checklist_tasks: Give plant a deep, thorough watering or bottom soak
Move to sheltered shade until foliage regains stiffness
Add top mulch layer to conserve soil moisture
Prune completely dead crispy leaves once recovered
